specification.title: GVE Level 3 Workflow Planning and Lifecycle

summary: GVE Level 3 Workflow Planning and Lifecycle defines complete workflow-plan construction and fail-closed acceptance, immutable accepted-plan binding, deterministic acyclic partial-order semantics, dependency and handoff validation, operation eligibility, attempt identity and ordering constraints, lifecycle-state distinctions, cancellation and timeout observation, retry requirements, partial-progress accounting, and workflow terminality without defining maintained scheduling implementation or evidence and result realization.

definitions.text: The pre-execution plan containing the single workflow identity, complete operation membership, unique operation identities, selected plugin and action bindings, exactly one fresh validated operation contract for every operation, the complete deterministic acyclic partial-order relation, dependency edges, handoff declarations, governing authority, and immutable registry and runtime snapshot identities.

The single fail-closed pre-execution determination that one complete workflow plan is internally consistent, deterministic, fully contracted, partial-order-valid, dependency- and handoff-valid, and eligible for lifecycle processing. Determinism does not require a unique topological serialization.
The uniquely identifiable immutable set of accepted plan, contract, registry, runtime, and authority facts governing one lifecycle attempt.
The complete deterministic graph of operation prerequisites whose identities, edges, and satisfaction conditions are uniquely attributable and valid for one accepted plan.

The accepted-plan declaration binding one producing operation, one consuming operation, one handoff identity, and the application-independent conditions required before the consumer can become eligible.

The fail-closed lifecycle determination that one operation may begin an attempt under the accepted plan because authority, required predecessor relations, dependencies, handoffs, contract freshness, and current lifecycle conditions are all satisfied.
A stable identifier unique within the workflow lifecycle and bound to exactly one operation identity, one accepted-plan snapshot, and one attempt ordinal.

The accepted-plan partial order governing which eligible operation attempts must precede which others. Eligible attempts not related by the partial order may be serialized or scheduled in more than one valid way without changing accepted-plan meaning.
The application-independent state of one operation or attempt, preserving distinct eligible, blocked, skipped, unattempted, attempted, interrupted, cancelled, timed-out, failed, and completed facts.
The lifecycle fact that a cancellation request was observed by the governed attempt, distinct from the request itself, interruption, terminal cancellation, and any effect claim.
The lifecycle fact that an applicable timeout condition was observed by the governed attempt, distinct from timeout configuration, interruption, terminal timeout, and any effect claim.

The fail-closed determination that explicit governing authority permits another attempt after a prior attempt and that all relevant plan, contract, registry, runtime, dependency, handoff, and lifecycle freshness conditions have been re-evaluated.

The complete representation of all operations and attempts that are terminal, nonterminal, blocked, skipped, unattempted, interrupted, or otherwise unresolved at a lifecycle observation point without converting lifecycle state into effect evidence.
The fail-closed determination that every operation and every created attempt has complete, consistent, uniquely attributable terminal lifecycle accounting.

requirements.text: One workflow-plan acceptance attempt must evaluate exactly one complete workflow plan containing the full operation membership, unique operation identities, selected plugin and action bindings, exactly one fresh validated operation contract per operation, all ordering constraints expressed as the complete partial-order relation, all dependency edges, all handoff declarations, governing authority, and immutable registry and runtime snapshots.

Workflow-plan acceptance must be one deterministic fail-closed pre-execution decision over the complete plan; missing, duplicate, conflicting, ambiguous, stale, unauthorized, incomplete, or non-uniquely attributable plan facts must reject acceptance before any operation is attempted.
An accepted plan must have one stable accepted-plan snapshot identity, and its operation, contract, authority, registry, and runtime facts must remain immutable for the governed lifecycle attempt.

Operation membership and ordering constraints must define one complete deterministic acyclic partial order over stable operation identities. Independent operations require no artificial ordering edge, and multiple topological serializations of the same accepted partial order are valid. Total-order position rules and rejection merely because more than one valid serialization exists must not be used to reject independent operations or impose artificial precedence. The plan must fail closed for missing operations, duplicate identities, unresolved operation references, self-ordering, conflicting or contradictory constraints, cycles, missing required sequencing, or ambiguous constraint meaning.

The dependency graph must identify every prerequisite edge and satisfaction condition uniquely, must reject unknown or duplicate operation identities, self-dependencies, conflicting edges, and prohibited cycles, and must remain immutable after plan acceptance.

Every lifecycle handoff declaration must bind exactly one producer operation, one consumer operation, one handoff identity, and explicit acceptance conditions; missing, duplicate, ambiguous, stale, incompatible, or non-uniquely attributable handoffs must fail closed.

Operation eligibility must be derived only from the accepted-plan snapshot, governing authority, valid fresh operation contract, deterministic ordering through satisfied predecessor constraints, satisfied dependencies, valid handoffs, and current lifecycle facts.

No operation attempt may be created or begun before operation eligibility is established; attempted execution without eligibility must fail closed and remain distinguishable from an authorized eligible attempt.

Every created attempt must have one fresh unique attempt identity bound to exactly one operation identity, one accepted-plan snapshot identity, and one deterministic attempt ordinal; identity reuse or ambiguous attribution must fail closed.

A scheduler or concrete topological serialization may choose among currently eligible attempts only within the accepted partial-order constraints and must not alter accepted-plan meaning, introduce an undeclared precedence edge, or be treated as part of accepted-plan identity. Scheduler choice, including any choice under unspecified concurrency, must not depend semantically on declaration order, discovery order, filesystem order, registry iteration order, validator iteration order, or process timing.

Eligible, blocked, skipped, unattempted, attempted, interrupted, cancelled, timed-out, failed, and completed lifecycle facts must remain distinct; no state may be inferred from another merely because both are terminal or prevent further work.
A cancellation request, cancellation observation, interruption caused by cancellation, and terminal cancelled state must be represented as distinct uniquely attributable lifecycle facts.
A timeout configuration or request, timeout observation, interruption caused by timeout, and terminal timed-out state must be represented as distinct uniquely attributable lifecycle facts.

Retry eligibility must require explicit governing authority, a fresh unique attempt identity, a new deterministic attempt ordinal, and re-evaluation of all relevant plan, contract, registry, runtime, dependency, handoff, and lifecycle freshness conditions.

Partial-progress accounting must include every operation and every created attempt with complete current lifecycle attribution and must not omit blocked, skipped, unattempted, interrupted, cancelled, timed-out, failed, or nonterminal facts.

Workflow terminality must be established only when every operation and every created attempt has complete, consistent, uniquely attributable terminal lifecycle accounting; unresolved, conflicting, missing, or ambiguous lifecycle facts must prevent terminality.

Workflow-plan acceptance, eligibility, attempt creation, blocking, skipping, cancellation, timeout, interruption, failure, completion, retry, and terminality are lifecycle facts only and must not by themselves establish requested, authorized, attempted, completed, observed, or verified effect claims.

This specification must not define detailed plugin or action contract fields, registration mechanics, action input interpretation, validated-operation-contract production, evidence schemas, evidence sufficiency, effect-claim realization, operation-result schemas, uncertainty semantics, or authoritative workflow-result assembly.

This specification must not define maintained runtime, scheduler, executor, queue, plugin, action, or registry implementation; language-specific state-machine or concurrency primitives; deployment, persistence, caching, performance, or distributed-coordination choices; bootstrap executor formats; or changes to accepted Levels 0 through 2.

includes: Complete workflow-plan construction and fail-closed acceptance
Immutable accepted-plan, contract, authority, registry, and runtime snapshot binding
Deterministic operation membership and acyclic partial-order constraints
Independent operations without artificial ordering edges
Operation eligibility and prohibition on premature attempts
Unique attempt identity and partial-order-constrained attempt eligibility
Distinct eligible, blocked, skipped, unattempted, attempted, interrupted, cancelled, timed-out, failed, and completed facts
Distinct cancellation and timeout request, observation, interruption, and terminal facts
Retry authority, fresh-attempt identity, and re-evaluation requirements
excludes: Maintained runtime, scheduler, executor, queue, plugin, action, and registry implementation
Concrete scheduler algorithms and topological-serialization policy
Language-specific state-machine, coroutine, thread, process, and concurrency primitives
Detailed plugin and action contract fields, registration mechanics, input interpretation, and validated-contract production
Evidence schemas, evidence sufficiency, effect-claim realization, operation-result schemas, uncertainty, and authoritative workflow-result assembly
Plugin-specific filesystem, command-execution, local-Git, remote-service, credential, and publication semantics
Deployment, persistence, caching, performance, and distributed-coordination choices
Bootstrap executor operation formats and implementation behavior
